newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels accused of seeking "final solution" for refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels accused of seeking "final solution" for refugees.

text.p: A U.N. aerial search confirmed Friday that some 85,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees fled into the Zairian jungle and aid agencies accused Tutsi-dominated rebels of seeking "a final solution" by condemning them to die.
"We didn't see any refugees," said Carlos Haddad, Kisangani represetantive of the U.N. World Food Program (WFP), after flying 58 miles south of Zaire's northeastern capital.

"The forest is so dense that either they are hiding somewhere or they went west to Opala," Haddad said of the 55,000 refugees who fled a camp at Kasese and 30,000 who left a camp at Biaro, 25 miles south of Kisangani.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said the search found traces that people passed further south of Biaro and Kasese toward Ubundu and very small numbers of people scattered on a road and smoke coming from the thick forest.

The UNHCR said earlier it had received reports suggesting Biaro had been emptied. A U.N. mission allowed to reach Kasese Thursday found no refugees, alive or dead, after the camp was sealed off for four days from aid workers and journalists.
A UNHCR spokeswoman said agencies were also blocked from Biaro but an aid worker trapped there Tuesday reported a train-load of rebels arriving followed by looting and fighting.
The aid worker said the Hutus left Biaro soon afterward and went south in an orderly manner. Opala, mentioned as a possible destination by the WFP's Haddad is 100 miles southwest of Kisangani.

Under increasing international pressure over their treatment of up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees, the rebels said former Rwandan Hutu troops and militiamen evacuated the Hutu refugees from Kasese this week and denied massacring any of them.

The refugees' are becoming a public relations disaster for rebel leader Laurent Kabila. But rebel officials accuse the media of biased reporting and blame U.N. agencies for not repatriating them earlier despite U.N. plans for an airlift being blocked until May 5.
In Geneva, aid agencies expressed outrage at rebel treatment of the refugees, who fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
"Eighty thousand people are condemned to a slow and cruel death. The expression 'final solution' is not exaggerated," said Christiane Berthiaume, spokeswoman for the World Food Program.
"They (the rebels) want these people to die. There's food over there but these people are starving. If the refugees go into the jungle, they will die. We are powerless," she added.
Kabila told Reuters in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi that he would invite the United Nations and aid agencies to investigate the crisis over Rwandan refugees in rebel areas.
"I seek nothing but the truth about the refugee crisis in Kisangani. I will immediately be asking the United Nations and aid agencies to set up an independent probe team on the saga," he said.

Kabila again repeated denials his forces had slaughtered Rwandan Hutu refugees at a camp south of the eastern provincial capital of Kisangani but said he would accept independent findings and where necessary take action against his troops.
The U.N. Security Council Thursday harshly criticized the rebels for preventing aid from reaching the Hutu refugees south of Kisangani and obstructing their return home to Rwanda.

Kabila said his forces, who have taken more than half of Zaire since October, could seize the town of Kikwit, 240 miles east of Kinshasa, within 48 hours and the battle for the capital would be swift.

He said he wanted face-to-face talks with President Mobutu Sese Seko in South Africa or possibly Zambia and rejected all other proposed venues on security grounds. The president has rejected South Africa.
Kabila did not mention Gabon as a venue for talks. Mobutu's son and spokesman said earlier the president had no objection to meeting Kabila there and the date depended on his father.
